punctuated:
獨苦者與？

賢者原音之所以美，而因著其為樂也。盖樂本諸音也，有是德音而後謂之樂，則樂豈易言哉？

子夏對魏文侯問樂，意謂樂與音相近而不同，君欲知樂，盍先知音乎？何則？聲者，音之所由成也。姦聲濫而音亡矣，尚何德音之足云？今既禮立於大當之餘，而樂正於大定之後，則被之聲律者，莫非人倫物理之所存；播之歌詩者，罔非妙道精義之所發。知聲可以知音矣，斯不謂之德音乎？謂之德音，則古樂固即此而在矣。何則？音者，樂之所由成也。溺音出而樂亡矣，尚何古樂之足云？今既終之無不可語，而用之無往不宜，則天地同和，而有以宣八風之氣；神人胥悅，而有以揚九叙之功。知音可以知樂矣，斯不謂之古樂乎？吁！古樂本於德音，則新樂之害德必矣。文侯顧問此而好彼，亦獨何哉？

抑論之，五帝不相沿樂，王者功成作樂，是樂者，帝王之德之所寓也。然非聖人，則亦莫能窮其妙。觀孔子之
translation_en:
…is he alone in taking such pains [?]?

The worthy man traces what makes tones beautiful and thereby makes clear how they constitute music. For music is rooted in tones: only when there are these virtuous tones can it be called music. How, then, could music be easy to discuss?

When Zixia answered Marquis Wen of Wei’s question about music, his meaning was that music and tones are closely related but distinct: “If you, my lord, wish to understand music, why not first understand tones?” Why is this? Sounds are that from which tones are formed. When corrupt sounds proliferate, tones perish; what virtuous tones would then remain to speak of? Now, once ritual has been established upon the attainment of complete propriety, and music rectified after complete order has been secured, everything clothed in measured sounds embodies human relationships and the principles of things; everything disseminated in songs and poems expresses the wondrous Way and its subtle meanings. By understanding sounds, one can understand tones. Is this not what is called “virtuous tones”? If they are called virtuous tones, then ancient music is surely present in them.

Why is this? Tones are that from which music is formed. When debauched tones emerge, music perishes; what ancient music would then remain to speak of? Now, when a performance has ended, there is nothing in it unfit for discussion, and wherever it is employed, it is appropriate. Thus Heaven and Earth share in harmony, allowing the vital energies of the winds from the eight directions to circulate; spirits and human beings alike rejoice, allowing the achievements of the nine ordered undertakings to be proclaimed. By understanding tones, one can understand music. Is this not what is called “ancient music”? Ah! Since ancient music is rooted in virtuous tones, the harm that new music does to virtue is certain. Yet Marquis Wen asked about the former while delighting in the latter. Why indeed was this?

To consider the matter further: the Five Emperors did not simply perpetuate one another’s music; kings created music when their achievements were complete. Music is thus that in which the virtue of emperors and kings resides. Yet only a sage can fully fathom its subtleties. Consider how Confucius…

translation_en:
…hearing the Shao music in Qi makes this clear. Alas, in later ages few understood virtue: not only could no one put ancient music to use, but even its lingering strains had almost vanished. This is truly lamentable! Nevertheless, had Marquis Wen acted upon Zixia’s words to rectify music, might he not have approached its abundant beauty? Regrettably, he was not fit to be addressed on this matter.
“Establishing love begins with one’s parents: this teaches the people to live in harmony. Establishing respect begins with one’s elders: this teaches the people obedience. Teach them kindness and harmony, and the people will prize having parents; teach them to respect their elders, and the people will prize obeying commands. Serve parents with filial devotion and heed commands with obedience: put these into practice throughout the realm, and nowhere will they fail to take effect.”
Liang Shoujian
Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Assistant Instructor: Love and respect are the foundation of ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the realm. Only by explaining these as one connected sequence does the meaning become complete. This composition achieves that.
Comment by Examiner Xie, Left Mentor: The four characters meaning “deepen what is near and extend it afar” encompass the entire chapter. This is someone who has given careful thought to the foundation from which good government proceeds.
Comment by Examiner Zhai, Academician: The explanation of how moral teaching is established is clear.
In discussing the teaching of filial devotion and fraternal deference, the Sage deepens what is near and extends it afar. For filial devotion and fraternal deference are the foundation of teaching the people. Once this teaching is established among those above, no place is too distant for it to reach. Is this not because its principles are shared by all human hearts? title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
始而已是故家有親也篤天性之恩而子道克
盡則愛立於上而所以教民睦者不于是乎家
有長也敦天倫之序而弟道克盡則敬立於上
而所以教民順者不于是乎惟其教之以睦故
同是愛者以心感心而莫不貴於有親一家仁
一國興仁焉惟其教之以順故同是敬者以德
感德而莫不貴於用命一家讓一國興讓焉夫
既孝以事親則立愛之教隨試而輒效矣順以
聽命則立敬之教無施而弗驗矣由是舉斯心
===
而措之通天下而一心無弗愛者以梗吾之化
殆風之偃草也舉此德而措之合天下而一德
無弗敬者以畔吾之治殆影之隨形也由是觀
之則愛敬之道為齊家治國平天下之本明矣
人君可不知所以先之乎抑聞之堯舜之道孝
弟而已矣親睦九族而萬邦協和慎徽五典而
四方風動其明驗也堯舜豈能强人以必從哉
亦不過盡已之性以盡人之性耳後世徒急於
知謀功利之末而德教無聞焉是無恠乎其治

…the beginning, and nothing more. Thus, within the household there are parents: when the ruler deepens the affection grounded in natural bonds and fully discharges his duties as a son, love is established above. Is this not how he teaches the people to live in harmony? Within the household there are elders: when he strengthens the order of the natural human relationships and fully discharges his duties as a younger brother, respect is established above. Is this not how he teaches the people obedience? Precisely because he teaches them harmony, those who share this love respond heart to heart, and all prize affection for their parents. When one household practices benevolence, a whole state is stirred to benevolence. Precisely because he teaches them obedience, those who share this respect respond virtue to virtue, and all prize compliance with commands. When one household practices deference, a whole state is stirred to deference.

Once he serves his parents with filial devotion, the teaching that establishes love proves effective whenever it is put to the test. When he obediently heeds their commands, the teaching that establishes respect proves effective wherever it is applied. By extending this heart and putting it into practice, he unites all under Heaven in one heart; none remain without love to obstruct his transforming influence. It is like the wind bending the grass. By extending this virtue and putting it into practice, he brings all under Heaven together in one virtue; none remain without respect to rebel against his government. It is like a shadow following a form. Viewed thus, the way of love and respect is clearly the foundation for ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven. Can a ruler fail to understand what he should put first?

Could Yao and Shun have compelled everyone to follow them without fail? They merely fulfilled their own nature in order to enable others to fulfill theirs. Reading it, one fears only that it will end. Surely its author has attained profound understanding?

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
高宗不得不重傅說而傅說見重於高宗亦無
所嫌矣
聖人任人以天下之重必先使之自重而後可
以有為矣天下至重也求其人以任之則固使
之負吾之重也使之負吾之重而不使之自重
以為之地則彼固不敢輕於自任而吾之所謂
重者弗克舉矣聖人知其然曰天下之重也吾
弗克自舉也求其人以任之無乃責之重乎要
亦使之自重而已矣故凡所以持其心養其望
===
者雖以身下之而不辭是故彼有以自重而吾
之所重者亦且舉之矣聖人任輔相之道如此
古之人有行之者高宗是也高宗之任傅說也
其始也恭默思道三年不言既而命之曰若歲
大旱用汝作霖雨若濟巨川用汝作舟楫若作
和羹用汝作鹽梅夫說一岩阿之叟也出于疎
遠拔于微賤高宗者一旦露肺肝出情愫若有
所不及焉者固將以任之也任之以負吾之所
重也天下者天下之天下也殺生予奪進退用

punctuated:
高宗不得不重傅說，而傅說見重於高宗亦無所嫌矣。

聖人任人以天下之重，必先使之自重，而後可以有為矣。天下至重也，求其人以任之，則固使之負吾之重也。使之負吾之重，而不使之自重以為之地，則彼固不敢輕於自任，而吾之所謂重者弗克舉矣。聖人知其然，曰：「天下之重也，吾弗克自舉也。求其人以任之，無乃責之重乎？要亦使之自重而已矣。」故凡所以持其心、養其望者，雖以身下之而不辭。是故彼有以自重，而吾之所重者亦且舉之矣。聖人任輔相之道如此。古之人有行之者，高宗是也。高宗之任傅說也，其始也，恭默思道，三年不言。既而命之曰：「若歲大旱，用汝作霖雨；若濟巨川，用汝作舟楫；若作和羹，用汝作鹽梅。」夫說，一岩阿之叟也，出于疎遠，拔于微賤。高宗者，一旦露肺肝，出情愫，若有所不及焉者，固將以任之也，任之以負吾之所重也。天下者，天下之天下也。殺生予奪、進退用
translation_en:
…Gaozong could not but accord weight to Fu Yue, and there was likewise nothing objectionable in Fu Yue’s being so esteemed by Gaozong.

When a sage entrusts someone with the weighty responsibility of all under Heaven, he must first enable that person to recognize his own worth; only then can anything be accomplished. All under Heaven is a responsibility of the utmost gravity. To seek a suitable person and entrust it to him is indeed to have him shoulder the ruler’s own burden. If the ruler has him shoulder that burden without enabling him to recognize his own worth as the foundation for doing so, the man will certainly not dare lightly to take it upon himself, and what the ruler regards as his weighty responsibility will remain unfulfilled. Understanding this, the sage says: “The burden of all under Heaven is one I cannot shoulder alone. If I seek a suitable person and entrust it to him, am I not imposing a heavy responsibility upon him? The essential thing is simply to enable him to recognize his own worth.” Thus, in whatever serves to sustain that man’s resolve and nurture his standing, the sage does not shrink even from placing himself below him. In this way, the man has grounds for valuing himself, and the ruler’s weighty responsibility can also be discharged. Such is the sage’s way of appointing chief ministers.

Among the ancients, Gaozong was one who put this into practice. Before appointing Fu Yue, he reverently maintained silence and pondered the Way, speaking not a word for three years. Then he charged him, saying: “Should the year bring a great drought, I would use you as the soaking rain. Should I cross a great river, I would use you as the boat and oars. Should I prepare a well-seasoned soup, I would use you as the salt and sour plums.” Now Yue was an old man from a rocky recess, brought forth from obscurity far from court and raised from a humble and lowly position. Gaozong suddenly laid bare his innermost thoughts and expressed his deepest feelings, as though afraid of falling short. Surely this was because he intended to entrust Yue with responsibility—to have him shoulder what the ruler himself regarded as his weighty burden. All under Heaven belongs to all under Heaven. Putting to death and granting life, bestowing and taking away, advancing and dismissing, employing…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
舎聖人之權也聖人不得而私之也其是非得
失可否之間盖與賢者共之也而榮辱利害進
退之節又賢者之所重也知賢者之所重而不
知所以重之則彼肯自貶以徇人乎固不屑也
不惟不屑抑亦有所不敢也任之不專也禮之
不重也上下之未交也羣議之弗附也固不敢
輕以其身自試乎危疑之地也是故賢者不敢
也不屑不敢而莫能有為則聖人抱天下之重
器悵悵焉無所於歸聖人之心窮矣是故思有
===
以重之非重其人也重其賢也重其賢以負吾
之所重也故其始也擇之不慎則知之不明知
之不明則信之不篤信之不篤則任之不專禮
之不厚而責之不重矣故未得其人則海宇之
未一也億兆之未寧也萬幾之未理也吾皆所
不屑也顧明揚之未盡也潜德之未升也考慎
之未至也吾是以憂之也及既得其人也擇之
既精則知之必明由是信之篤而疑貳顧慮無
所懐也任之專而謀猷器能無不盡也禮之厚

translation_en:
…and dismissing: these are powers of the sage ruler, yet he may not exercise them for his private ends. In deciding what is right or wrong, beneficial or harmful, permissible or impermissible, he shares deliberation with worthy men. Honor and disgrace, advantage and harm, and the proper occasions for entering or withdrawing from office are, in turn, matters that worthy men take seriously. If one knows what worthy men value but does not know how to accord them due weight, would they willingly lower themselves to accommodate others? They would certainly disdain to do so. Nor is it merely a matter of disdain: there are also things they dare not do. When they are not entrusted with undivided responsibility, when they are not treated with due ceremony, when ruler and minister have not established mutual understanding, and when general opinion does not support them, they certainly dare not lightly put themselves to the test in a precarious and uncertain position. This is why worthy men dare not act. If, through disdain or apprehension, they cannot accomplish anything, then the sage ruler holds the weighty vessel of the realm in his arms, distressed and with no one to whom he can entrust it. His mind has reached an impasse. Thus he considers how to accord them due weight. It is not their persons that he honors, but their worthiness; he honors their worthiness so that they may bear the weighty responsibilities that are his.

Thus, at the outset, if he does not choose carefully, he will not understand them clearly; if he does not understand them clearly, he will not trust them firmly; if he does not trust them firmly, he will not entrust them with undivided responsibility, treat them with ample ceremony, or charge them with weighty duties. Therefore, before obtaining the right man, he thinks: “That the realm is not yet unified, that its countless people are not yet at peace, and that the myriad affairs of government are not yet in order—none of these is what I concern myself with. Rather, that the search for and promotion of worthy men has not been exhaustive, that men of hidden virtue have not been raised to office, and that careful scrutiny has not been carried to its utmost—these are my concerns.” Once he has obtained the right man, his selection having been exacting, his understanding must be clear. Hence he trusts him firmly, harboring neither doubt nor misgivings; he entrusts him with undivided responsibility, so that his plans, abilities, and talents are all fully employed; he treats him with ample ceremony…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而勢望尊重莫敢揺也責之重而切於自任功
可成也夫然後任之以至誠弗敢疑也隆之以
師禮弗敢臣也坐之以論道弗敢慢也故賢者
自知其任之重也禮之隆也君臣之交孚也羣
議之弗奪也則挺然以其身自任天下之重也
高宗之時何時也荆楚之未平也諸侯之未服
也刑賞僭濫王室之不振也故高宗之言曰以
台正于四方也台恐德之弗類也所以負天下
之重者汲汲也於是求所謂說者而任之懼其
===
無以負吾之重也恭默思道三年不言慎之至
也賚于上帝徵于物色篤于旁求擇之精也乃
命之曰若濟巨川用汝作舟楫如險之望脫也
若歲大旱用汝作霖雨如苗之欲搞也若作和
羹用汝作鹽梅如五味之相和雖欲缺一而不
可也盖知之明也信之篤也任之專也禮之厚
也責之重也而相須倚賴若是之急且切也是
以任重而不可辭也勢尊而不可揺也交深而
不可間也由是納誨以輔德也啓心以沃心也

無以負吾之重也恭默思道三年不言愼之至
也賚于上帝徴于物色篤于旁求擇之精也乃
命之曰若濟巨川用汝作舟楫如險之望脱也
若歲大旱用汝作霖雨如苗之欲槁也若作和
羮用汝作鹽梅如五味之相和雖欲缺一而不
可也蓋知之明也信之篤也任之專也禮之厚
也責之重也而相須倚頼若是之急且切也是
以任重而不可辭也勢尊而不可揺也交深而
不可間也由是納誨以輔德也啓心以沃心也
punctuated:
而勢望尊重，莫敢揺也；責之重，而切於自任，功可成也。夫然後任之以至誠，弗敢疑也；隆之以師禮，弗敢臣也；坐之以論道，弗敢慢也。故賢者自知其任之重也，禮之隆也，君臣之交孚也，羣議之弗奪也，則挺然以其身自任天下之重也。
高宗之時，何時也？荆楚之未平也，諸侯之未服也，刑賞僭濫，王室之不振也。故高宗之言曰：「以台正于四方也，台恐德之弗類也。」所以負天下之重者汲汲也。於是求所謂說者而任之，懼其無以負吾之重也。恭默思道，三年不言，慎之至也；賚于上帝，徵于物色，篤于旁求，擇之精也。乃命之曰：「若濟巨川，用汝作舟楫。」如險之望脫也。「若歲大旱，用汝作霖雨。」如苗之欲搞也。「若作和羹，用汝作鹽梅。」如五味之相和，雖欲缺一而不可也。盖知之明也，信之篤也，任之專也，禮之厚也，責之重也，而相須倚賴若是之急且切也。是以任重而不可辭也，勢尊而不可揺也，交深而不可間也。由是納誨以輔德也，啓心以沃心也。
translation_en:
…and his standing and prestige are so exalted that none dares shake them; the responsibilities laid upon him are weighty, and he earnestly takes them upon himself, so that success can be achieved. Only then does the ruler entrust him with duties in perfect sincerity, not daring to doubt him; honor him with the courtesies due a teacher, not daring to treat him as a mere subject; and seat him to discuss the Way, not daring to slight him. Thus the worthy man knows that his responsibilities are weighty, that the honors accorded him are exalted, that ruler and minister trust one another, and that others’ opinions cannot overturn his appointment. He then resolutely takes upon himself the weight of all under Heaven.
What sort of time was the age of Gaozong? Jingchu had not been pacified, the regional lords had not submitted, punishments and rewards were presumptuously and indiscriminately administered, and the royal house had not regained its strength. Thus Gaozong said: “Through me the four quarters are to be set right, yet I fear that my virtue is unequal to the task.” He was urgently concerned about bearing the weight of all under Heaven. Accordingly, he sought the man called Yue and entrusted him with office, fearing that this man might lack the means to bear the burden that was his own. Reverently silent, he pondered the Way and did not speak for three years: this was the utmost caution. Yue was bestowed upon him by the Lord on High; he verified him by his appearance and searched earnestly far and wide: this was meticulous selection. He then charged him, saying: “If I am to cross a great river, I shall use you as my boat and oars.” This was like someone in danger longing to escape. “If the year brings a great drought, I shall use you as the soaking rain.” This was like seedlings longing for moisture [?]. “If I am to make a well-seasoned soup, I shall use you as salt and sour plums.” This was like blending the five flavors: even if one wished to omit a single one, one could not. His understanding of Yue was clear, his trust profound, his delegation of authority undivided, his courtesies generous, and the responsibilities he imposed weighty; his need for and reliance upon Yue were thus urgent and pressing. Therefore Yue’s responsibilities were too weighty to decline, his position too exalted to shake, and his bond with the ruler too deep for anyone to come between them. Accordingly, he offered admonitions to assist the ruler’s virtue, and opened his own heart to nourish the ruler’s heart…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聰明欲其憲天也建事欲其師古也典學欲其
務時敏也成憲欲其監先王也舉天下之事莫
不以身任其重蕩蕩然無所顧慮而必其成功
此高宗之所以中興也故曰聖人任輔相之道
也抑高宗之任傅說重也抑何以必知其良而
重之邪曰典學之功也觀其命說之言曰予小
子舊學于甘盤則凡用人行政之道是非邪正
之辨亦聞之素矣此其傅岩一聘而慇懃委重
如此也顧其學終罔顯而不若虞廷股肱耳目
===
之言相資猶一體也及其得說之後開導之深
乃命之曰股肱惟人良臣惟聖則其所造益深
切矣若高宗者其幾於聖者也三代而下漢唐
宋諸君始無典學之功遂乏知人之鑒其在當
時所以任輔相者吾不得而知也故以漢高之
英宗臣猶繫之暴以唐太宗之賢而君臣之好
不終則其他又可知也此三代之治所以不復
也

punctuated:
聰明欲其憲天也，建事欲其師古也，典學欲其務時敏也，成憲欲其監先王也。舉天下之事，莫不以身任其重，蕩蕩然無所顧慮，而必其成功，此高宗之所以中興也。故曰：聖人任輔相之道也。抑高宗之任傅說重也，抑何以必知其良而重之邪？曰：典學之功也。觀其命說之言曰：「予小子舊學于甘盤。」則凡用人行政之道，是非邪正之辨，亦聞之素矣。此其傅岩一聘，而慇懃委重如此也。顧其學終罔顯，而不若虞廷股肱耳目之言，相資猶一體也。及其得說之後，開導之深，乃命之曰：「股肱惟人，良臣惟聖。」則其所造益深切矣。若高宗者，其幾於聖者也。三代而下，漢唐宋諸君始無典學之功，遂乏知人之鑒。其在當時所以任輔相者，吾不得而知也。故以漢高之英，宗臣猶繫之暴；以唐太宗之賢，而君臣之好不終，則其他又可知也。此三代之治所以不復也。

表
translation_en:
…In intelligence and discernment, he wished him to model himself on Heaven; in undertaking affairs, to follow antiquity; in steadfast study, to apply himself diligently and promptly; and in established institutions, to take the former kings as his mirror. In all the affairs of the realm, he personally shouldered their weight, acting with expansive confidence, free of misgivings, and determined to achieve success. This was how Gaozong brought about a restoration. Thus I say: this was the sage’s way of entrusting responsibilities to his chief ministers.

Yet Gaozong entrusted Fu Yue with weighty responsibilities. How could he be certain of his worth and place such weight upon him? The answer is: through the achievement of steadfast study. Consider his words when he charged Yue: “I, the young one, formerly studied under Gan Pan.” He had thus long been instructed in the principles of employing men and conducting government, and in distinguishing right from wrong and perversity from rectitude. This explains why, upon summoning Fu Yue from Fuyan, he so earnestly entrusted him with weighty responsibilities. Yet his learning had still failed to become manifest: it had not reached the mutual reliance, like that of a single body, expressed in the words about limbs, ears, and eyes at the court of Shun. After obtaining Yue and receiving his profound guidance, he charged him, saying: “As limbs make a man complete, so worthy ministers make a sage complete.” His attainment had thereby become still deeper and more thorough. Gaozong was surely one who approached sagehood.

After the Three Dynasties, the rulers of Han, Tang, and Song lacked from the outset the achievement of steadfast study, and consequently lacked the discernment needed to judge men. I cannot comprehend the way they entrusted responsibilities to their chief ministers in their day. Thus, despite the brilliance of Gaozu of Han, an eminent minister still associated him with violence [?]; despite the worthiness of Taizong of Tang, the affection between ruler and ministers did not endure to the end. From these examples, the others may also be understood. This is why the good government of the Three Dynasties was never restored.

Memorial

Draft Congratulatory Memorial from the Assembled Officials on the Sacred Festival of Imperial Longevity
Yang Yue
Associate Examiner Liang, Assistant Instructor, comments: “This memorial expresses the utmost loyalty and love of a subject for his ruler, leaving almost nothing unexpressed. It should be copied out and presented to the throne.”
Examiner Xie, Left Assistant Mentor, comments: “A fine memorial.”
Examiner Zhai, Academician, comments: “It achieves the proper form for blessings and praise.”
Your servants, so-and-so and others, holding their respective offices, state: On the tenth day of the eighth month of the fourth year of Jiajing, we reverently encounter the Sacred Festival of Imperial Longevity. With utmost joy and delight, we bow our heads to the ground and repeatedly kowtow as we submit these words.
We humbly consider: As blessings attend the Imperial Ultimate, all lands look up to the benevolence that distributes them abroad; joyfully meeting this auspicious day, we emulate, across a thousand years, the spirit of answering one another in song. Pouring out our humble sincerity, we turn toward the sun of Your Majesty and pray that your long life may equal Heaven’s. Our rites forgo elaborate ornament; our feelings are those of all who join in the dance.
We humbly reflect that the emergence of emperors and kings is indeed bound up with the flourishing of cosmic forces and fortune. Whatever is to unfold must have its precursors; nothing departs without returning. When the house of Yu arose, …

translation_en:
…a red rainbow manifested an auspicious portent; when the Shang dynasty began, a dark bird descended as a favorable sign. Examining the true portents through the ages, we find that the transmission and reception of sovereignty were never matters of private preference in seeing and hearing. Consulting the enduring rites, we find that praise has always been rooted in honoring and loving one’s parents. Thus it was in antiquity; today it is especially flourishing.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, like Shun of redoubled splendor, accords with the sovereign before him, and that Heaven’s appointed succession rests upon your person. Your excellence was already manifest while the dragon remained hidden; your divinely aided rise was foretold by the appearance of clouds. The three luminaries converged auspiciously, the sun’s course fulfilling the portent of its position in the Horn lodge; the Four Waterways displayed their spiritual power, and the Huai region presented a hymn celebrating the Yellow River’s running clear. August Heaven bestowed its favor and mandate; all within the realm gave you their allegiance. You embody the vigor of Qian, Heaven, to preside over the people; facing the brightness of Li, Fire, you attend to government. Your utmost benevolence brings tranquility; your great filial devotion is beyond description. Taking established statutes as your mirror, you remain forever free of error; mindful of both end and beginning, you apply yourself constantly to learning. You rejoice with all under Heaven…

translation_en:
…its radiance fittingly like the sun at noon. The occasion of rejoicing for the One Man coincides with the season when the myriad treasures of the earth yield their bounty. Joyful acclamations shake the earth; harmonious vapors rise as clouds. As Heaven’s blessings newly unfold, you ever cherish your august father in carrying forward his undertakings; as wine cups are raised together, shared delight fills the apartments of your gracious mother. Moreover, the accomplishment of your transforming influence confirms the divination of intertwined madder roots [an omen of worthy men advancing together], while your cultivated brilliance foretells an auspicious, pure sacrificial offering. Great peace has its visible signs; like Heaven and Earth, you shelter and sustain all without partiality. The many officials are truly harmonious, as at the court of Shun; the four numinous creatures all arrive, as in the royal park of Zhou.

We, your servants, are fortunate to share in this encounter with your reign, and most earnestly look up to you in devoted reliance. Emulating the blessings proclaimed at Mount Song, we raise three acclamations, deeming paltry the Tang courtier’s rhapsody on Qing Shan, “Celebrating Goodness.” Bowing amid the ranks of officials, arrayed like phoenixes, we make a hundred obeisances, finding inadequate the Han court’s ceremonial at Changle Palace. 聖祖。功德之隆，卓冠萬世。此作鋪張揚厲，本末不遺，豈所謂賢者識其大者邪？

同考試官教諭陳批：我聖祖治功之盛，本於聖德，前代帝王之所不能及者，正在於此。是策敷陳詳悉，而末復歸重於聖學，可謂善觀聖人者矣。

同考試官教諭廖批：聖製一策，正見我聖祖創業垂統之盛。是篇敷對詳明，末復以守法之勸為聖天子望，忠愛溢於言表矣。他日揚于王庭，必有將順以為聖德之助，豈獨為科目之重而已邪？

考試官左贊善謝批：我聖祖德冠古今，功兼創守，非前代帝王所及，此發問意也。子能一言中的，而終篇之獻復出忠悃，蓋深於菁莪棫樸之化者矣。允宜高薦。
translation_en:
…the Sagely Founder. The grandeur of his achievements and virtue stands preeminent through all ages. This composition expansively celebrates them, omitting neither their foundations nor their ramifications. Is this not what is meant by saying that the worthy recognize what is greatest?

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: The magnificent achievements of our Sagely Founder’s government were rooted in his sagely virtue. Precisely here lay what emperors of earlier dynasties could not match. This policy essay expounds the matter thoroughly and in detail, and at its close again places the chief emphasis on sagely learning. Its author may indeed be called a discerning observer of the sage.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liao, Instructor: This imperially composed policy question reveals precisely the magnificence of our Sagely Founder’s establishment of the dynasty and transmission of its rule to posterity. This essay responds fully and clearly. At its close, it further expresses the hope that our sagely Son of Heaven will heed the exhortation to uphold the established laws; loyalty and devotion overflow its words. When its author is one day advanced to the royal court, he will surely support and further the ruler’s good intentions, thereby assisting his sagely virtue. Could he merely bring distinction to the examination system?

Comment by Examiner Xie, Left Mentor: Our Sagely Founder’s virtue surpasses that of all ages, and his achievements encompass both founding and preserving the dynasty—something emperors of earlier dynasties could not match. This is the intent of the question. You have struck the mark with a single statement, while the counsel offered at the end of your essay also springs from sincere loyalty. You have evidently been deeply imbued with the transforming cultivation celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood” (Jing e) and “Dense Oaks” (Yu pu). You certainly deserve recommendation with a high ranking.

有聖人之全德，有聖人之全功。盖德者，功之本也；功者，德之表也。德有不備，不足以為發揮之地，而功用之全，烏有不根諸本原之地者哉？此我太祖高皇帝德冠古今，功兼創守，而非前代帝王之所可及也與！請因明問而敢陳之。自古帝王之有天下也，不惟創業之難，抑亦貽謀之不易。盖其混合之勢，雖麤定於草昧之餘，而經緯之功，不能不待於數傳之後。如漢高祖之興也，除秦滅項，伐暴安民，興縞素之師，立三章之約，其得天下可謂正矣，其規模可謂宏且遠矣。然而天下既定，頒之條教，施之號令，如命叔孫通起禮儀、韓信申軍法、蕭何次律令，徒振舉其大綱，而未盡乎詳密。故挾書之令，至文帝而……
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Zhai, Academician: Laws and institutions are the outward manifestation of moral virtue. Our sagely founder’s plans to secure the welfare of his descendants found their proper realization precisely here. This essay probes the foundations and traces matters to their source, understanding the subtle unity of the two. Its author’s cultivation is therefore far from ordinary or shallow.

With the complete virtue of a sage comes the complete achievement of a sage. Virtue is the foundation of achievement; achievement is the outward expression of virtue. If virtue is incomplete, it cannot provide a basis for its full expression. How could completeness of achievement and practical effect fail to be rooted in that fundamental source? This is why our Emperor Taizu Gao surpassed all past and present in virtue and combined the achievements of founding and preserving a dynasty, beyond the reach of emperors and kings of earlier ages! Permit me, in response to your illuminating question, to venture an explanation.

Since antiquity, when emperors and kings have possessed all under Heaven, founding their enterprise has not been their only difficulty; leaving plans for their successors has also been no easy matter. Although unification might be roughly secured in the aftermath of the initial turmoil, the work of ordering the realm necessarily awaited several successive reigns. Consider the rise of Gaozu of Han: he swept away Qin, destroyed Xiang Yu, attacked the violent, and brought peace to the people. He raised an army clad in white mourning garments and established a compact of three articles. His acquisition of the realm may be called legitimate, and the framework he laid down may be called grand and far-reaching. Yet once the realm was settled, the regulations he promulgated and the commands he issued—such as ordering Shusun Tong to establish ceremonial observances, Han Xin to set forth military regulations, and Xiao He to arrange the statutes and ordinances—merely put the broad outlines into effect without achieving thoroughness in detail. Thus the edict prohibiting possession of books, only in the reign of Emperor Wen…

punctuated:
後除，表章之功歷建元而始盛。吕祿、吕產擅權分亂，外戚之無制也；南軍、北軍矯持符節，軍政之無統也；惠皇仁柔，政歸房闥，而預教之無方；七國叛亂，幾危社稷，而封建之無術。史雖稱其日不暇給，要之，馬上之論、猛士之歌，帝之所得止於是矣，安望其萬目之能盡舉也哉！
洪惟我太祖高皇帝驅逐胡元，受天明命，掃除自古所未有之腥羶，而復帝王所自立之中國。其得天下之正，固有非漢高帝所可及者。况適丁勝國之季，冠屨倒置之餘，彝倫攸斁，習俗圯壞極矣。其擾攘叢集、洗濯爬剔之勞，其視漢高帝之時又何如也？然而宸極未定，即思所以與天下維新；大命既集，日圖所以與斯民更始。是以彌綸經緯、運量於聖心者，大綱舉于上，萬目備于下。施之當時，為定功保業之規；傳之後世，為持盈守成之
translation_en:
…only then was it abolished; the work of honoring and promoting classical learning did not begin to flourish until the Jianyuan reign period. Lü Lu and Lü Chan monopolized power and fomented disorder: the imperial in-laws were subject to no restraints. Credentials of command were fraudulently wielded over the Southern and Northern Armies: military administration lacked unified authority. Emperor Hui was benevolent but weak, and government fell into the hands of the inner palace: there had been no proper method of educating the heir beforehand. The rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms nearly imperiled the altars of soil and grain: there had been no sound method for establishing the feudatory kingdoms. Although the histories say that the emperor could scarcely cope with each day's demands, in essence his understanding extended no further than the discussion of ruling from horseback and the song about mighty warriors. How could one expect him to attend fully to every detail?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao expelled the alien Yuan and received Heaven's illustrious mandate. He swept away a rank and fetid pollution unprecedented since antiquity and restored the central realm in which emperors and kings had established their rule. The righteousness with which he won the realm was assuredly beyond anything Emperor Gao of Han could match. Moreover, he encountered the closing years of the preceding dynasty, after a time when caps and shoes had exchanged places—when the proper social order had been overturned. The enduring human relationships had fallen into decay, and customs had become utterly corrupted. With turmoil and troubles massing together, how did the labor of cleansing and rooting out abuses compare with that of Emperor Gao of Han? Yet even before his imperial throne was secure, he was already considering how to renew the realm; once the great mandate had come to him, he planned daily how to make a fresh beginning with the people. Thus, through the comprehensive ordering and deliberation of his sagely mind, the main principles were established above and every detail was provided for below. Applied in his own time, these became rules for securing his achievements and preserving his enterprise; transmitted to later generations, they became means of maintaining prosperity and safeguarding what had been accomplished…

聖政記
大明日曆
寶訓諸書儒臣之序記而得其槩矣如敬天則
立圜丘方澤以秩百神之祀如勤民則令
屬民讀法而行鄉飲之儀
正儲位以立青宮所以定大本也

卒皆護衛其權皆統於
===

惟期于止辟刑法明矣

保富貴而兵權不使與家法之嚴也他如

計。愚生嘗莊誦《聖政記》《大明日曆》《寶訓》諸書、儒臣之序記，而得其槩矣。如敬天，則立圜丘、方澤，以秩百神之祀；如勤民，則令屬民讀法，而行鄉飲之儀。正儲位以立青宮，所以定大本也；封諸王而鎮天下，所以昭大分也。自京師郡國，卒皆護衛，其權皆統於朝廷，軍政肅矣。取前代律例，損益折中，其制惟期于止辟，刑法明矣。
皇明有訓，昭鑒有錄，所以立義方之教者無不嚴；郡縣有學，頒賜有書，所以敦造士之法者無不備。諸司有定制，而革其冗濫，倖位無不清；嶽瀆去封號，而題以某神，禮儀無不正。后妃居中壺，而朝政不敢干，内則之正也；外戚保富貴，而兵權不使與，家法之嚴也。他如
translation_en:
…plans. I, an unworthy student, have reverently read such works as the Record of Sagely Government (Shengzheng ji), the Daily Record of the Great Ming (Da Ming rili), and the Precious Instructions (Baoxun), together with the prefaces and accounts written by Confucian officials, and have thereby grasped their general outline. To reverence Heaven, he established the Circular Mound and the Square Marsh altars, putting the sacrifices to the hundred spirits in proper order. To care diligently for the people, he ordered that they be assembled to hear the laws read aloud and that the ceremonies of communal drinking be performed. He regularized the position of the heir apparent and established the crown prince’s palace, thereby securing the great foundation. He enfeoffed the princes to guard the realm, thereby making clear the great distinctions of rank. From the capital to the prefectures and princely domains, the soldiers all served as guards [?], and authority over them was centralized at court: military administration was thus disciplined. He took the statutes and precedents of earlier dynasties, making additions and reductions to achieve a balanced system, with the sole aim of bringing punishment to an end: penal law was thus made clear.
The August Ming had its Instructions, and the Illuminating Mirror its Record: every measure for establishing instruction in righteousness was rigorous. Prefectures and counties had schools, and books were bestowed upon them: every provision for strengthening the training of scholars was complete. The various offices had fixed regulations, and superfluous posts and excessive appointments were abolished, clearing away all positions obtained through favoritism. The sacred peaks and waterways were stripped of their bestowed titles and designated simply as the spirit of the place concerned: ritual observances were thus fully rectified. Empresses and consorts resided in the inner palace [the transcription is doubtful here] and dared not interfere in court government: this exemplified the correctness of the rules governing the inner quarters. Imperial relatives by marriage retained their wealth and honors but were not allowed to share military authority: this exemplified the strictness of the dynastic household rules. Other examples include…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
冠服有制防範有法民志無僣差矣朝貢
有期賜賚有節四夷皆賓從矣凡一建立
一設施真足以為天地立心為生民立命
為萬世
聖子神孫開燕翼之謀豈漢高帝所能彷彿哉
所以然者盖由
天厭夷德篤生
聖人聰明睿知之資本於天縱剛健中正之德
冠乎百王故其立心之宏慮事之遠凡其
===

才高世之智有不能外焉者夫豈偶然之

冠服有制，防範有法，民志無僣差矣。朝貢有期，賜賚有節，四夷皆賓從矣。凡一建立、一設施，真足以為天地立心，為生民立命，為萬世聖子神孫開燕翼之謀，豈漢高帝所能彷彿哉？
所以然者，盖由天厭夷德，篤生聖人，聰明睿知之資本於天縱，剛健中正之德冠乎百王。故其立心之宏、慮事之遠，凡其所建立，皆至精而至備，盡善而盡美。故百餘年来，内外守畫一之政，其樞機品式，循之則治，失之則亂。雖有絕倫之才、高世之智，有不能外焉者，夫豈偶然之故哉？

translation_en:
…Caps and robes have prescribed forms, and safeguards have established rules; thus the people harbor no aspirations to usurp rank or depart from their proper stations. Tribute missions have appointed times, and imperial gifts have regulated limits; thus the barbarians of the four quarters all submit as subjects. Every institution founded and every measure implemented truly suffices to establish the heart of Heaven and Earth, to establish the destiny of the living people, and to lay plans for the security of his sagely sons and divine grandsons through ten thousand generations. How could Emperor Gao of the Han even approach this achievement?
The reason is that Heaven, having grown weary of the virtue of the barbarians, brought forth a sage richly endowed. His gifts of perception and sagacious wisdom were bestowed by Heaven; his virtues of strength, vigor, centrality, and rectitude surpassed those of all former kings. Thus, such were the breadth of his intentions and the foresight of his deliberations that everything he established was supremely refined and comprehensive, perfectly good and perfectly beautiful. Hence, for more than a hundred years, officials at court and in the provinces have maintained a uniform system of government. Following its essential mechanisms, standards, and forms brings order; departing from them brings disorder. Even those of incomparable talent and surpassing wisdom cannot go beyond them. How could this possibly be accidental?
Furthermore, I, in my humble understanding, have reverently contemplated the greatness of our sagely founder’s achievements in government. These were certainly grounded in the completeness of his sagely virtue, while the completeness of his sagely virtue was itself rooted in the essentials of sagely learning. For example…

punctuated:
宮中無事，則觀孔子《論語》之言；內殿新成，則書古人行事於壁；註《尚書·洪範》，以為帝王之要道；揭《大學衍義》，以備朝夕之覽觀，則所以開發聖聰、資益神智者，為益深矣。功德之盛，有由然哉！《書》曰：「有典有則，以貽子孫。」聖祖有焉。《詩》云：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」愚生敢請以為聖天子獻。
第二問
査懋光
同考試官教諭尤批
帝王心學之要，士子類能言之，然皆摭拾陳言，泛濫成篇。此作舉《大學》明德之言，祖虞廷精一之訓，援古證今，不迂不激，可以為聖學勸矣。
translation_en:
…when there was no business in the palace, he would read the words of Confucius in the Analects; when a new inner hall was completed, he would inscribe the deeds of the ancients upon its walls. He annotated the “Great Plan” chapter of the Book of Documents, taking it as the essential Way for emperors and kings, and displayed the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi) for his reading morning and evening. Thus the means by which he enlarged his sagely understanding and enriched his divine wisdom became ever more profound. Surely the greatness of his achievements and virtue had its source! The Book of Documents says: “There are statutes and rules to be handed down to descendants.” Our sagely founding ancestor possessed these. The Book of Odes says: “Neither transgressing nor forgetting, follow the old statutes.” I, an ignorant student, venture to ask leave to offer these words to our sagely Son of Heaven.

Second Policy Question
Zha Maoguang 査懋光

Comment by Associate Examiner You 尤, Instructor:
Candidates generally can discuss the essentials of the learning of the mind for emperors and kings, yet they merely gather stale sayings and fill their essays with rambling verbiage. This composition cites the Great Learning’s words on luminous virtue, takes as its foundation the court of Shun’s instruction to be discerning and single-minded, and invokes antiquity to substantiate its arguments about the present. Neither impractical nor intemperate, it can serve to encourage His Majesty’s sagely learning.

占子之所學矣
考試官左贊善謝批心為萬化之原論
聖學而必歸諸心人皆知之至於援筆成文不冗不泛而深得聖賢
相傳之要者無踰此篇

===
帝王之為治本於學帝王之為學本於心
蓋為治而不本於學則治無其本固無以
成化理之功為學而不本於心則學非其
要徒從事於言語文字之間不惟無益於
治且有以累乎治矣古帝王之學豈如是
哉執事發策秋闈舉帝王之學下詢愚生

Yet for writing that is neither verbose nor diffuse, and that profoundly grasps the essentials transmitted from sage to sage and worthy to worthy, nothing surpasses this essay.

The governance of emperors and kings is rooted in learning; the learning of emperors and kings is rooted in the mind. For if governance is not rooted in learning, it lacks its foundation and assuredly cannot achieve the work of moral transformation and good order. If learning is not rooted in the mind, it misses what is essential and merely occupies itself with words and writings. Not only does this fail to benefit governance; it may even encumber it. Could the learning of the ancient emperors and kings have been like this?

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
明君以務學為急盖人君一身天地祖宗
之所付托四方萬民之所仰賴萬幾庶政
之所叢委其是非邪正得失之幾見於用
人行政揆事宰物之間紛紜而不可禦混
殽而不可辨然非義理所存纖悉畢照則
何以得其當然之實而應天下之務哉是
故明君以務學為急而學也者又非尋章
摘句誇多闘靡者之所為也嘗聞之大學
之教矣曰在明明德在新民帝王之學不
===
越乎此二者而已何謂明明德先之格物
致知以開其端繼之誠意正心以致其實
而其原則本於唐虞之授受觀堯之授舜
曰允執厥中舜之授禹復益以三言曰人
心惟危道心惟微惟精惟一允執厥中而
宋儒朱熹釋之曰精則察乎二者之間而
不雜即格物致知之謂也一則守其本心
之正而不離即誠意正心之謂也故胡氏
謂此十六字開萬世心學之淵源豈不然

之教矣曰在明明德在新民帝王之學不
===
越乎此二者而已何謂明明德先之格物
致知以開其端繼之誠意正心以致其實
而其原則本於唐虞之授受觀堯之授舜
曰允執厥中舜之授禹復益以三言曰人
心惟危道心惟微惟精惟一允執厥中而
宋儒朱熹釋之曰精則察乎二者之間而
不雜即格物致知之謂也一則守其本心
之正而不離即誠意正心之謂也故胡氏
謂此十六字開萬世心學之淵源豈不然
punctuated:
「明君以務學為急。」盖人君一身，天地祖宗之所付托，四方萬民之所仰賴，萬幾庶政之所叢委。其是非邪正得失之幾，見於用人行政、揆事宰物之間，紛紜而不可禦，混殽而不可辨。然非義理所存，纖悉畢照，則何以得其當然之實，而應天下之務哉？是故明君以務學為急。而學也者，又非尋章摘句、誇多闘靡者之所為也。嘗聞之《大學》之教矣，曰：「在明明德，在新民。」帝王之學，不越乎此二者而已。
何謂明明德？先之格物致知，以開其端；繼之誠意正心，以致其實。而其原則本於唐虞之授受。觀堯之授舜，曰：「允執厥中。」舜之授禹，復益以三言，曰：「人心惟危，道心惟微，惟精惟一，允執厥中。」而宋儒朱熹釋之曰：「精則察乎二者之間而不雜。」即格物致知之謂也。「一則守其本心之正而不離。」即誠意正心之謂也。故胡氏謂此十六字開萬世心學之淵源，豈不然
translation_en:
…“An enlightened ruler regards dedication to learning as an urgent priority.” For the ruler, in his single person, bears what Heaven, Earth, and his ancestors have entrusted to him; he is the one upon whom the myriad people throughout the realm depend, and in whom the countless affairs and duties of government converge. The subtle beginnings of right and wrong, perversity and rectitude, success and failure appear amid the employment of men, the conduct of government, the assessment of affairs, and the governance of all things. They are so multitudinous that they cannot be mastered, so intermingled that they cannot be distinguished. Yet unless he illuminates every last detail wherever moral principles reside, how can he grasp what truly ought to be done and respond to the affairs of the realm? Thus an enlightened ruler regards dedication to learning as an urgent priority. Such learning, moreover, is not the practice of those who hunt through chapters and pick out phrases, boast of their extensive knowledge, and compete in literary embellishment. I have heard it in the teachings of the Great Learning: “It lies in manifesting luminous virtue and in renewing the people.” The learning of emperors and kings goes no further than these two things.
What is meant by manifesting luminous virtue? One begins with investigating things and extending knowledge, thereby making a start; one follows this with making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind, thereby bringing it to fulfillment. Its source lies in the transmission between the rulers of Tang and Yu. Consider what Yao said when transmitting rule to Shun: “Sincerely hold fast to the Mean.” When Shun transmitted rule to Yu, he added three further phrases: “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle. Be discerning and be single-minded; sincerely hold fast to the Mean.” The Song Confucian Zhu Xi explained: “To be discerning is to distinguish between these two without confusing them.” This is what is meant by investigating things and extending knowledge. “To be single-minded is to preserve the rectitude of one’s original mind without departing from it.” This is what is meant by making the intentions sincere and rectifying the mind. Thus Master Hu said that these sixteen characters opened the wellspring of the learning of the mind for all ages. Is this not indeed so…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
乎自是而後聖聖相承如成湯之以義制
事以禮制心文王之緝熙敬止小心翼翼
武王敬怠義欲之辨刀劔户牖之銘作聖
之功雖有不同精一之傳則一而已帝王
之學舎是豈復有他道哉故在當時黎民
之於變萬邦之咸寧聲教之四訖兆民之
允殖三分之有二四海之永清治效極於
一時休烈垂於萬世迥乎其不可及也三
代而下英君誼辟非不知學如招選茂異
===
表章六經漢武之功大矣然多欲一念幾
踵亡秦有得於人心道心之辨者能如是
乎受經尚書能通大義光武之學偉矣然
人倫之間不能無憾有得於天敘天秩之
道者固如是乎唐太宗身屬櫜鞬銳情經
術而挾父臣虜手刃同氣何貴於弘文之
討論玄宗延禮文儒發揮典籍而任用林
甫竟致播遷何貴於更日之侍讀宋太宗
夜分觀書手不釋卷而宋后之不成其服

夜分觀書手不釋卷而寡后之不成其服
punctuated:
乎？自是而後，聖聖相承，如成湯之以義制事、以禮制心，文王之緝熙敬止、小心翼翼，武王敬怠義欲之辨、刀劔户牖之銘，作聖之功雖有不同，精一之傳則一而已。帝王之學，舎是豈復有他道哉？故在當時，黎民之於變、萬邦之咸寧、聲教之四訖、兆民之允殖、三分之有二、四海之永清，治效極於一時，休烈垂於萬世，迥乎其不可及也。

三代而下，英君誼辟非不知學。如招選茂異，表章六經，漢武之功大矣。然多欲一念，幾踵亡秦，有得於人心道心之辨者能如是乎？受經《尚書》，能通大義，光武之學偉矣。然人倫之間不能無憾，有得於天敘天秩之道者固如是乎？唐太宗身屬櫜鞬，銳情經術，而挾父臣虜，手刃同氣，何貴於弘文之討論？玄宗延禮文儒，發揮典籍，而任用林甫，竟致播遷，何貴於更日之侍讀？宋太宗夜分觀書，手不釋卷，而宋后之不成其服
translation_en:
…is this not so? Thereafter, sage succeeded sage. Cheng Tang regulated affairs through righteousness and his mind through ritual propriety; King Wen continued to illuminate his virtue, abiding in reverence and exercising utmost care; King Wu distinguished reverence from negligence and righteousness from desire, and had admonitions inscribed on knives, swords, doors, and windows. Although their efforts to become sages differed, the transmission of discerning concentration and single-mindedness was one and the same. Could there be any other path for the learning of emperors and kings? Thus, in their respective times, the common people were transformed, the myriad states all enjoyed peace, their civilizing influence reached the four quarters, the multitude truly prospered, two of the realm’s three parts came under one ruler, and all within the Four Seas enjoyed lasting tranquility. Their achievements in government reached their height in their own times, and their glorious accomplishments were handed down for ten thousand generations. How far beyond reach they stand!

After the Three Dynasties, outstanding sovereigns and righteous rulers were by no means ignorant of learning. Emperor Wu of Han accomplished much by recruiting men of exceptional talent and promoting the Six Classics. Yet his propensity for multiplying desires nearly led him to follow Qin into ruin. Could someone who understood the distinction between the human mind and the mind of the Way have acted thus? Emperor Guangwu received instruction in the Book of Documents and grasped its great principles: his learning was impressive. Yet his conduct within human relationships was not without cause for regret. Would someone who understood Heaven’s ordering of relationships and ranks really have acted thus? Taizong of Tang wore a bow case and quiver upon his person and devoted himself eagerly to classical learning. Yet he coerced his father, treating him as a captive subject [?], and slew his own brothers with his own hand. What value, then, lay in the scholarly discussions at the Hongwen Academy? Xuanzong welcomed and honored literary scholars and elucidated the canonical writings. Yet he employed Linfu and ultimately was driven into flight. What value, then, lay in having scholars attend him to expound texts on alternating days? Taizong of Song read late into the night, never putting down his books; yet full mourning rites were not observed for Empress Song…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
二王之不得其終慚德多矣高宗潛心聖
經專講春秋而甘心君父之讐淪棄中原
之地遺譏遠矣之數君者或泥於章句之
間而不知脩己治人之大道徒事於文詞
之末而不知反身踐履之實功故其所就
如是而已安敢望其治之古若哉仰惟我
聖天子登極之初首御經筵
即位以來緝熈聖學邇者復
詔儒臣編輯經史直解以進仰窺
===
聖心真有得乎帝王之傳而遠探淵源之妙矣
執事欲舉其要以仰裨
緝熈之萬一而要之一言愚生已陳之矣豈有
外於虞廷精一之訓大學明德之功哉蓋
人之一心雖微而實管乎天下之理理雖
散在萬事而實本於人之一心况乎萬幾
之繁事物之變可喜可欲日交於前而察
理有未精守善有不固則是非易以眩惑
物欲易以轉移而念慮之間不能不小失

二王之不得其終，慚德多矣。高宗潛心聖經，專講春秋，而甘心君父之讐，淪棄中原之地，遺譏遠矣。之數君者，或泥於章句之間，而不知脩己治人之大道；徒事於文詞之末，而不知反身踐履之實功。故其所就如是而已，安敢望其治之古若哉？仰惟我聖天子登極之初，首御經筵；即位以來，緝熈聖學。邇者復詔儒臣編輯經史直解以進，仰窺聖心，真有得乎帝王之傳，而遠探淵源之妙矣。
執事欲舉其要，以仰裨緝熈之萬一，而要之一言，愚生已陳之矣。豈有外於虞廷精一之訓、大學明德之功哉？蓋人之一心雖微，而實管乎天下之理；理雖散在萬事，而實本於人之一心。况乎萬幾之繁、事物之變，可喜可欲，日交於前，而察理有未精，守善有不固，則是非易以眩惑，物欲易以轉移，而念慮之間不能不小失
translation_en:
…and the two princes failed to meet a proper end: many were the blemishes upon his virtue. Gaozong devoted his mind to the sages’ classics and concentrated on expounding the Spring and Autumn Annals, yet acquiesced in leaving his sovereign and father unavenged and abandoned the lands of the Central Plain, bequeathing grounds for enduring reproach. These several rulers [?] either became mired in textual divisions and phrases, without understanding the great Way of cultivating oneself and governing others, or merely occupied themselves with the peripheral refinements of literary expression, without understanding the substantial work of examining oneself and putting learning into practice. Thus their accomplishments amounted to no more than this. How could one dare hope that their government would match that of antiquity? Reverently considering our sagely Son of Heaven, at the very beginning of his accession he gave priority to attending the Classics Colloquium; ever since taking the throne, he has continually extended and illuminated his sagely learning. Recently he again commanded his Confucian officials to compile Plain Explanations of the Classics and Histories for presentation to him. Reverently discerning his sagely intentions, we see that he has truly grasped the transmission of the ancient emperors and kings and reached far back to probe the subtleties of its source.
You, honored examiners, wish to bring forward its essentials so as to contribute even the smallest measure to this continued illumination of learning. Yet the single statement that sums up those essentials is one that I, your unworthy student, have already set forth. Could anything fall outside the instruction to be discerning and single-minded given at the court of Shun, or the work of illuminating luminous virtue taught in the Great Learning? Though a person’s mind is subtle, it in fact encompasses all the principles under Heaven; though principle is dispersed among the myriad affairs, it is in fact rooted in the individual mind. Moreover, amid the complexity of the myriad affairs of government and the changes of things and events, objects that delight and excite desire daily present themselves before one. If one’s discernment of principle is not sufficiently refined and one’s adherence to goodness is not firm, one can easily become confused about right and wrong and be swayed by material desires, so that in one’s thoughts one cannot avoid slightly losing…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其正矣故必先讀書窮理格物致知以盡
事物之變然後修身體道誠意正心以收
踐履之功師于古訓凡聖賢之告戒其操
存省察者何居考于前史凡漢唐宋諸君
之政治其是非得失者安在不必泛濫以
為博惟精察夫天理人欲之幾不必記誦
以為工惟允蹈乎身體力行之實日積月
累自明而誠推之用人行政之間達夫應
事接物之際內外昭融表裏澄徹而可以
===
應天下之務矣唐虞三代之治遠而不可
追者吾未之信也抑愚於此又有說焉聖
學固以正心為要尤以得賢為輔蓋賢人
君子所以講明義理維持此心者也尤願
聖天子旁求俊彥大召名儒列侍從之司陪
清閒之燕則切劇啟沃
聖學益增於廣大薰陶漸染
聖性益進於高明矣愚生末學管見如斯執事
倘以為然用以為

聖性益進於高明矣愚生末學管見如斯執事

punctuated:
其正矣。故必先讀書窮理，格物致知，以盡事物之變，然後修身體道，誠意正心，以收踐履之功。師于古訓，凡聖賢之告戒，其操存省察者何居？考于前史，凡漢唐宋諸君之政治，其是非得失者安在？不必泛濫以為博，惟精察夫天理人欲之幾；不必記誦以為工，惟允蹈乎身體力行之實。日積月累，自明而誠，推之用人行政之間，達夫應事接物之際，內外昭融，表裏澄徹，而可以應天下之務矣。唐虞三代之治，遠而不可追者，吾未之信也。
抑愚於此又有說焉：聖學固以正心為要，尤以得賢為輔。蓋賢人君子，所以講明義理、維持此心者也。尤願聖天子旁求俊彥，大召名儒，列侍從之司，陪清閒之燕，則切劇啟沃，聖學益增於廣大；薰陶漸染，聖性益進於高明矣。愚生末學，管見如斯。執事倘以為然，用以為
translation_en:
…its rectitude. Thus one must first read books and fathom principles, investigate things and extend knowledge, so as fully to comprehend the changes of affairs and things; then cultivate oneself and embody the Way, make one’s intentions sincere and rectify one’s mind, so as to achieve results in actual practice. Taking ancient teachings as one’s model, one should ask: in all the admonitions of sages and worthies, wherein lie the methods for preserving the mind and examining oneself? Examining earlier histories, one should ask: in the government of the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song, where lay their right and wrong, their successes and failures? One need not range indiscriminately through texts to claim breadth of learning, but should discern precisely the subtle distinction between heavenly principle and human desires. One need not make memorization and recitation the measure of proficiency, but should truly fulfill the substance of personal practice and strenuous action. Through daily accumulation over months, one proceeds from understanding to sincerity, extending this to employing men and conducting government, and applying it when responding to affairs and dealing with things. When inward and outward are luminous and harmonious, and surface and substance clear throughout, one can respond to the affairs of the world. I do not believe that the good government of Yao and Shun and the Three Dynasties is so remote that it cannot be attained again.
Yet I, in my ignorance, have something further to say. Sagely learning certainly takes rectification of the mind as its essential task, but it particularly requires the assistance of worthy men. For worthy men and gentlemen elucidate moral principles and sustain this mind. I especially hope that the sagely Son of Heaven will seek outstanding men far and wide, summon eminent Confucian scholars in great numbers, appoint them to attendant offices, and have them accompany him in his moments of quiet leisure. Through earnest and urgent counsel [?], they will enlighten and nourish him, and his sagely learning will grow ever broader and greater; through their gradual, formative influence, his sagely nature will advance ever further in loftiness and illumination. Such is the narrow view of this humble student of meager learning. If you, honored officials, consider it sound, use it as…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
緝熙之助亦區區芹曝之誠也
第三問
陳經
同考試官訓導劉批求循吏於久任之
餘此自古良法類為好進者沮壞故每有建白而終
不行此答援大易通變之說而歸於勢與情之難行者
欲愛惜體恤以權之的然有見末復致嘆於好惡之偏切
中時弊真有用之文哉
同考試官教諭康批說吏治處不盜襲陳言
===
專以通變為論能通其變則任人立法皆在其中觀此足
以占子用世之學
考試官左贊善謝批吏治一策正驗經生用世之
志子以使民宜之立說而歷指今日不能久任之弊痛快人情
錄之不獨以其文也
考試官學士翟批久任之法類能言之而其中
調停潤澤不随衆是非自得之學也
君子欲善吏治于天下亦惟使民宜之而
已矣民無不宜于吏之久□吏不能久則

以占子用世之學
考試官左贊善謝　批〔吏治一策正驗經生用世之志子以使民宜之立說而歷指今日不能久任之弊痛快人情〕
錄之不獨以其文也
考試官學士翟　批〔久任之法類能言之而其中調停潤澤不隨衆是非自得之學也〕
君子欲善吏治于天下亦惟使民宜之而
已矣民無不宜于吏之久□吏不能久則
punctuated:
緝熙之助，亦區區芹曝之誠也。
第三問，陳經。
同考試官訓導劉批：求循吏於久任之餘，此自古良法，類為好進者沮壞，故每有建白而終不行。此答援大易通變之說，而歸於勢與情之難行者，欲愛惜體恤以權之，的然有見。末復致嘆於好惡之偏，切中時弊，真有用之文哉！
同考試官教諭康批：說吏治處不盜襲陳言，專以通變為論。能通其變，則任人立法皆在其中。觀此足以占子用世之學。
考試官左贊善謝批：吏治一策，正驗經生用世之志。子以使民宜之立說，而歷指今日不能久任之弊，痛快人情。錄之不獨以其文也。
考試官學士翟批：久任之法，類能言之，而其中調停潤澤，不随衆是非，自得之學也。
君子欲善吏治于天下，亦惟使民宜之而已矣。民無不宜于吏之久□，吏不能久則
translation_en:
…as an aid to the continued illumination of imperial learning, this too expresses my humble sincerity in offering such poor gifts as cress and the sun’s warmth.
Third Policy Question. Chen Jing.
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Assistant Instructor: Seeking conscientious officials through prolonged tenure is a sound method handed down from antiquity. Yet those eager for advancement commonly obstruct and undermine it; hence proposals are repeatedly submitted but ultimately never implemented. This answer invokes the teaching of the great Book of Changes on adapting to change, and locates the difficulty of implementation in circumstances and human feelings. Its wish to temper the policy with care and sympathetic consideration shows definite insight. At the end it again laments partiality in likes and dislikes, striking directly at the abuses of our time. Truly an essay of practical use!
Comment by Associate Examiner Kang, Instructor: In discussing official administration, he does not plagiarize stale pronouncements, but bases his argument entirely on adapting to change. If one can respond appropriately to change, both appointing men and establishing regulations are encompassed within this. This essay suffices to reveal your learning for service in the world.
Comment by Examiner Xie, Left Mentor: A policy essay on official administration is precisely a test of a classical scholar’s aspiration to serve the world. You base your argument on ensuring that the people find the arrangements suitable, and enumerate the present abuses that prevent officials from remaining long in office. This gives satisfying expression to people’s feelings. We have selected it for more than its literary merit alone.
Comment by Examiner Zhai, Academician: Most can speak about the system of prolonged tenure, but the judicious adjustments and refinements proposed here, without following the crowd’s judgments of right and wrong, show learning independently attained.
If the gentleman wishes to improve official administration throughout the realm, he need only ensure that it suits the people. There are no people who do not benefit from officials’ prolonged [tenure?]. If officials cannot remain long in office, then…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
雖有愛民之心惠民之政亦皆倉卒苟且
匪徒無益而反害之是民不宜于吏之久
者非良民也吏不久宜於民者非循吏也
然則欲吏治之善于天下烏可不通其變
而徒泥其法以病乎民哉愚嘗讀易而有
以知聖人之言無往不在也其曰通其變
使民不倦神而化之使民宜之聖人何以
必求宜於民哉民不宜則倦矣又曰窮則
變變則通通則久道豈有窮哉通變其窮
===
則久矣執事發策慨循吏之不多見無乃
有望於司任人者體易之義而通其變與
粤稽唐虞建官首重民牧觀其命辭食哉
惟時柔遠能邇惇德允元而難任人責之
可謂厚矣觀其立法三載考績三考黜陟
幽明任之可謂久矣通變以作其倦神化
以致其宜此道之所以不窮而成垂衣之
治不獨用人然也三代封建之法行而民
宜於治嬴秦郡縣之制起而治不宜於民

有望於司任人者體易之義而通其變與
===
粤稽唐虞建官首重民牧觀其命辭食哉
惟時柔遠能邇惇德允元而難任人責之
可謂厚矣觀其立法三載考績三考黜陟
幽明任之可謂久矣通變以作其倦神化
以致其宜此道之所以不窮而成垂衣之
治不獨用人然也三代封建之法行而民
宜於治嬴秦郡縣之制起而治不宜於民
punctuated:
雖有愛民之心、惠民之政，亦皆倉卒苟且，匪徒無益，而反害之。是民不宜于吏之久者，非良民也；吏不久宜於民者，非循吏也。然則欲吏治之善于天下，烏可不通其變，而徒泥其法以病乎民哉？愚嘗讀《易》，而有以知聖人之言無往不在也。其曰：「通其變，使民不倦；神而化之，使民宜之。」聖人何以必求宜於民哉？民不宜則倦矣。又曰：「窮則變，變則通，通則久。」道豈有窮哉？通變其窮，則久矣。執事發策，慨循吏之不多見，無乃有望於司任人者體《易》之義而通其變與？
粤稽唐虞建官，首重民牧。觀其命辭：「食哉惟時，柔遠能邇，惇德允元，而難任人。」責之可謂厚矣。觀其立法：「三載考績，三考黜陟幽明。」任之可謂久矣。通變以作其倦，神化以致其宜，此道之所以不窮而成垂衣之治，不獨用人然也。三代封建之法行，而民宜於治；嬴秦郡縣之制起，而治不宜於民。
translation_en:
…even if officials have hearts that cherish the people and policies that benefit them, everything will be done hastily and perfunctorily, bringing not merely no benefit but actual harm. Thus, people who find an official’s long tenure unsuitable are not good people; officials who cannot remain beneficial to the people over a long tenure are not benevolent officials. If we wish official administration throughout the realm to be good, how can we fail to adapt to changing circumstances, and instead cling rigidly to established rules, to the people’s distress? I have read the Book of Changes and thereby come to understand that the sages’ words apply everywhere. It says: “Adapt to changing circumstances so that the people do not grow weary; transform them with wondrous efficacy so that things suit them.” Why must the sages seek what suits the people? If things do not suit them, they grow weary. It also says: “When possibilities are exhausted, change occurs; through change comes free passage; through free passage comes endurance.” How could the Way ever be exhausted? By adapting when its possibilities are exhausted, one achieves endurance. In setting this policy question, you gentlemen lament the scarcity of benevolent officials. Is it perhaps your hope that those responsible for appointing men will embody the meaning of the Book of Changes and adapt to changing circumstances?
Looking back to the establishment of offices under Tang and Yu, we find that foremost importance was placed on shepherds of the people. Consider the words of their commission: “Food! Attend to it at the proper time. Be gentle toward those far away and win over those nearby; honor the virtuous and trust the good, but keep crafty men at a distance.” The responsibilities imposed on them may indeed be called weighty. Consider the rules established: “Every three years, assess achievements; after three assessments, dismiss the benighted and promote the enlightened.” Their tenure may indeed be called long. Adapting to change revived those who had grown weary, and wondrous transformation brought about what suited them. This is why the Way was never exhausted and government was achieved with the ruler merely letting his robes hang down. Nor did this apply only to the employment of men. When the system of enfeoffment of the Three Dynasties prevailed, the people found their government suitable; when the system of commanderies and counties arose under the Ying house of Qin, government did not suit the people.

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
理亂之判有由然矣炎漢之興髙帝用蕭
曹之清靜以反秦敝光武解王莽之繁密
以還漢舊賢良孝廉之並舉刺史守相之
親覈選舉之科不一而同於為民考課之
法不一而同於務實至於久任之法或褒
其美而止增祿秩或終其身而遂長子孫
故循吏之著稱者西漢六人文翁王成輩
是也他若吳公之守河南何並焉東漢十
二人衛颯任延輩是也他若杜詩之守南
===
陽奚媿焉然當其時鼓舞之術雖亦足以
宜民而治功之成終不免於雜伯視古之
民牧蓋有不可同日而語者矣我
朝任人敷政動倣周官而損益之得中深體
易義而變通之有道是宜
祖宗之時吏民相安而化行俗美也夫何法弊
日滋人心日玩神而化之此其時乎以選
舉言之科貢之外復有薦舉之條求賢固
無類矣今如格例之太拘何苟能公以行

punctuated:
理亂之判有由然矣。炎漢之興，髙帝用蕭曹之清靜以反秦敝，光武解王莽之繁密以還漢舊。賢良孝廉之並舉，刺史守相之親覈，選舉之科不一而同於為民，考課之法不一而同於務實。至於久任之法，或褒其美而止增祿秩，或終其身而遂長子孫。故循吏之著稱者，西漢六人，文翁王成輩是也；他若吳公之守河南，何並焉？東漢十二人，衛颯任延輩是也；他若杜詩之守南陽，奚媿焉？然當其時，鼓舞之術雖亦足以宜民，而治功之成終不免於雜伯，視古之民牧，蓋有不可同日而語者矣。
我朝任人敷政，動倣周官，而損益之得中；深體易義，而變通之有道。是宜祖宗之時吏民相安，而化行俗美也。夫何法弊日滋，人心日玩？神而化之，此其時乎？以選舉言之，科貢之外復有薦舉之條，求賢固無類矣。今如格例之太拘何？苟能公以行
translation_en:
…The divergence between order and disorder thus had its reasons. When the Han dynasty, associated with the power of Fire, arose, Emperor Gao employed the quiet, noninterventionist approach of Xiao He and Cao Shen to reverse the abuses of Qin. Emperor Guangwu dismantled Wang Mang’s elaborate and exacting regulations to restore the old Han institutions. Men of worth and goodness and men noted for filial devotion and integrity were recommended together; regional inspectors, commandery governors, and chancellors of princedoms were personally scrutinized. The categories of selection differed, but all served the people; the methods of evaluating performance differed, but all sought substantive results. As for keeping officials long in office, some were commended for their excellence and merely received increases in salary and rank; others served for life, with favor extending to their descendants [?]. Thus, among those renowned as exemplary officials, there were six under the Western Han, including Wen Weng and Wang Cheng. Among others, who could rival Lord Wu in his governance of Henan? There were twelve under the Eastern Han, including Wei Sa and Ren Yan. Among others, what cause had Du Shi, as governor of Nanyang, to feel inferior to them? Yet although the means of encouraging officials at that time could benefit the people, their achievements in government were ultimately still mixed with the methods of hegemons. Compared with the shepherds of the people in antiquity, they could hardly be spoken of in the same breath.
In appointing men and administering government, our dynasty consistently models itself on the Offices of Zhou, striking the proper balance in its modifications. It profoundly grasps the meaning of the Book of Changes and adapts institutions according to the proper Way. It was therefore fitting that, under our imperial ancestors, officials and people lived together in harmony, moral transformation spread, and customs were excellent. Why, then, do institutional abuses multiply daily and people’s hearts grow ever more negligent? Is this not the time to effect transformation with spiritual efficacy? Regarding recruitment, beyond the examination and tribute routes there are also provisions for recommendation: the search for worthy men is certainly not confined to a single category. Yet what is to be done about the excessive rigidity of the present regulations and precedents? If only they could be administered impartially…

translation_en:
…them, then room for freedom from rigid restrictions still remains. As for evaluating officials, besides their court audiences there are also provisions for assessing outstanding performance: the appraisal of ability is indeed grounded in actual achievement. Yet what is to be done about excessive fixation on paperwork today? If these provisions can be administered impartially, room for avoiding such fixation still remains. Thus, the scarcity of exemplary officials is assuredly the fault of failing to retain them long in office. Consider appointments today: some officials are promoted three times in a single year; others are transferred twice before completing their term. The people, knowing that an official will not stay long, vie in deception and flattery, while the expense of seeing officials off and welcoming their successors becomes incalculable. Officials, knowing that they will not stay long, readily grow negligent, and cannot avoid private ambitions for further advancement. What is the state's purpose in appointing officials? That the resulting abuses should reach such a point—is this not cause for boundless dismay!
Some say: “Men enter official service at different times. As earlier and later entrants succeed one another, it is difficult to institute new rules governing the pace of advancement. Such are the circumstances.” In my humble view, however, no circumstances are beyond remedy. If one constantly cherishes and conserves talent, there will be enough able men; with enough able men, advancement may be rapid or slow. Some say: “Service involves both arduous and easy duties. Since both kinds must be shared, assignments to the capital and the provinces should be distributed equitably. Such are human feelings.” In my humble view, however, no feelings are beyond accommodation. If one constantly shows consideration, men's minds will be at ease; with their minds at ease, they may serve either in the capital or in the provinces. Once those above have sufficient talent at their disposal and those below are each content, why should long tenure be impracticable, or exemplary officials remain scarce? title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
行之而民自不病者盖此意也抑愚聞之
循之為義上順天理下順人情之謂也然
此類非浮薄苛刻者之所能而寬厚簡靜
之士又每苦於好承奉者之所不取奈之
何哉然則明好惡之分示趨向之的使化
續羔羊而陋兩漢於不足言斯固在司任
人者加之意焉以仰副我
上用賢愛民之盛心耳不知執事亦有取於
芻蕘之言否乎
===
第四問
楊𤉧
同考試官訓導梁 批 文係於習而好名之習
尤為背道是誠不可無所以倡率之者經生識此可以占

考試官學士翟 批 以一士子能知聖人不得已

行之，而民自不病者，盖此意也。抑愚聞之，循之為義，上順天理，下順人情之謂也。然此類非浮薄苛刻者之所能，而寬厚簡靜之士，又每苦於好承奉者之所不取，奈之何哉？然則明好惡之分，示趨向之的，使化續《羔羊》，而陋兩漢於不足言，斯固在司任人者加之意焉，以仰副我上用賢愛民之盛心耳。不知執事亦有取於芻蕘之言否乎？

楊𤉧
同考試官訓導梁批：文係於習，而好名之習尤為背道，是誠不可無所以倡率之者。經生識此，可以占其志矣。高薦何忝？
考試官左贊善謝批：聖賢之道具於六經，則六經為文章之祖明矣。子因論文而知所歸重，又引六經之數，以見聖賢之所以為文，可謂知道者矣。
考試官學士翟批：以一士子，能知聖人不得已
translation_en:
…put it into practice, and the people would naturally suffer no harm: this, I believe, is the intended meaning. I have also heard that “exemplary” conduct means conforming above to heavenly principle and below to human feeling. Yet frivolous and harsh men cannot achieve such conduct, while generous, tolerant, unassuming, and tranquil gentlemen repeatedly suffer rejection by those who favor obsequious service. What can be done? Clearly distinguish what is approved from what is condemned, and show the proper goal toward which to strive, so that moral transformation may continue that celebrated in “The Lamb’s Fur,” making even the achievements of the two Han dynasties seem too paltry to mention. Those responsible for appointing men must give this their attention, thereby fulfilling our sovereign’s lofty intention to employ the worthy and cherish the people. I wonder whether you, sir, might find anything worth adopting in these words of a humble grass-cutter and wood-gatherer.

Fourth Policy Question
Yang Jiao [?] (楊𤉧)

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Assistant Instructor: Writing depends on acquired habits, and the habit of seeking fame is particularly contrary to the Way. There must indeed be some means of providing leadership and guidance in this matter. That a student of the Classics recognizes this allows us to discern his aspirations. How could recommending him highly be undeserved?

Comment by Examiner Xie, Left Assistant Mentor: The Way of the sages and worthies is fully embodied in the Six Classics; thus it is clear that the Six Classics are the origin of literary composition. In discussing writing, you recognize where primary importance belongs. You also invoke the several Six Classics [?] to show why the sages and worthies wrote. You may indeed be called one who understands the Way.

Comment by Examiner Zhai, Academician: As a mere examination candidate, he can recognize that the sages had no alternative…

text:
而為文則其文可知矣宜冠本房
道具於心也而著之存乎文文係於習也
而一之存乎人甚矣文不可以易為也正
大奇靡之分而道之顯晦時之汙隆見之
由是知聖賢不得已而為文要其意雖一
言之微不可忽也然則世之為文者豈可
不心於明道而上之人又豈可不一其習
以袪好名之弊也哉請因明問而陳之鴻
蒙既判天地顯自然之文日月星辰山川
===

圖洛書是也時降于三代文備夫六經溫
柔敦厚詩教也疏通知遠書教也廣博易
良樂教也絜靜精微易教也恭儉莊敬禮

於明道為體不同而同於正大六經之外
信無文矣孔子生而刪述之功垂憲萬世
暴秦出而坑焚之罪上通於天漢高之興
雖不事詩書而正脉猶存習尚近古故以

道具於心也，而著之存乎文；文係於習也，而一之存乎人。甚矣，文不可以易為也！正大奇靡之分，而道之顯晦、時之汙隆見之。由是知聖賢不得已而為文，要其意，雖一言之微不可忽也。然則世之為文者，豈可不心於明道，而上之人又豈可不一其習，以袪好名之弊也哉？請因明問而陳之。鴻蒙既判，天地顯自然之文，日月星辰、山川草木是也。聖人迭作，天下著燦然之道，河圖洛書是也。時降于三代，文備夫六經。溫柔敦厚，《詩》教也；疏通知遠，《書》教也；廣博易良，《樂》教也；絜靜精微，《易》教也；恭儉莊敬，《禮》教也；屬辭比事，《春秋》教也。立教不同，而同於明道；為體不同，而同於正大。六經之外，信無文矣。孔子生而刪述之功垂憲萬世；暴秦出而坑焚之罪上通於天。漢高之興，雖不事詩書，而正脉猶存，習尚近古，故以
translation_en:
…and composed writings, the quality of his own writing can be inferred. He deserves first place in this examining section.

The Way is fully present in the heart, but its manifestation depends upon writing. Writing depends upon acquired habits, but bringing those habits into accord depends upon people. How far writing is from something that can be undertaken lightly! The distinction between the upright and grand and the eccentric and ornate reveals whether the Way is manifest or obscured, and whether the age is debased or flourishing. From this we know that sages and worthies wrote only when they could not do otherwise. In seeking their meaning, we must not neglect even the smallest utterance. How, then, can those who write in this world fail to devote their hearts to illuminating the Way? And how can those above fail to bring their habits into accord, thereby dispelling the pernicious pursuit of fame? Allow me to set this forth in response to your discerning question.

Once primordial chaos had divided, heaven and earth displayed their natural patterns: the sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, plants, and trees. As sages arose in succession, the resplendent Way became manifest in the world: the River Chart and the Luo Writing exemplify this. By the time of the Three Dynasties, writing found its full expression in the Six Classics. Gentleness and kindness, sincerity and generosity: these are the teachings of the Classic of Poetry. Broad understanding and knowledge of the distant past: these are the teachings of the Classic of Documents. Breadth of mind, ease, and goodness: these are the teachings of the Classic of Music. Purity and stillness, precision and subtlety: these are the teachings of the Classic of Changes. Respectfulness and frugality, dignity and reverence: these are the teachings of the Classic of Rites. Arranging words and juxtaposing events: these are the teachings of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Their teachings differ, yet all illuminate the Way; their literary forms differ, yet all are upright and grand. Beyond the Six Classics, there is truly no writing worthy of the name.

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
文為職以文論政以文講學者後先相望
而道之載諸經籍者亦賴之以復明也嗣
是再盛于唐極盛于宋習尚少異文體頓
殊然其間足以鳴世者愚也求之漢得一
人焉董子是也求之唐得一人焉韓子是
也求之宋得一人焉歐陽子是也然天人
之對原道之作論性之言先儒指摘以為

不同體裁亦異其視三子盖有間矣然純
乎操存而不移於習染又孰有過於周程

洪惟我
translation_en:
…those who made letters their profession, discussed government through writing, and expounded learning through writing appeared in succession. Through them, too, the Way recorded in the canonical writings was brought to light once more. Thereafter, letters flourished again under the Tang and reached their fullest flourishing under the Song. Prevailing practices differed somewhat, while literary forms differed markedly. Yet among those whose voices could resound throughout their age, I humbly find one in the Han: Master Dong, Dong Zhongshu; one in the Tang: Master Han, Han Yu; and one in the Song: Master Ouyang, Ouyang Xiu. Nevertheless, earlier Confucian scholars pointed out faults in the Responses on Heaven and Humanity, the essay An Inquiry into the Way, and the statements on human nature; contemporary scholars followed their lead and freely disparaged them. Although these works overcorrected errors and could not escape faults of inconsistency with the Way, they were largely sound, with only minor blemishes, and ultimately shared an upright and great purpose. These were the men who sustained letters [?] after the Three Dynasties.

Others, such as Ban Gu, Liu Xiang, and Ma Rong in the Han; Liu Zongyuan, Lu Zhi, and Yang Cheng in the Tang; and Sima Guang, Fan Zhongyan, and Lü Zuqian in the Song, differed in their views and in their literary forms. There was, it would seem, some distance between them and those three masters. Yet in the purity with which they held fast to and preserved the moral mind, unmoved by habitual influences, who could surpass the four masters Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu? Their discharge of official duties, their memorials and responses at court, and their discussions with teachers and friends are recorded in writings, all plainly there to see. They intended to illuminate the Way, and the Way became clear; they had no intention of establishing a reputation, yet their names became renowned. These surely are the models that writers of later ages ought to follow.

人貢舉之所以得士一惟經術是尚而詞

詩教而不失之愚崇書教而不失之誣崇
樂教而不失之奢崇易教而不失之賊崇
禮教而不失之煩崇春秋教而不失之亂
因文以觀其人因習以觀其世則當時之
所以化導而倡率之者誠不可誣矣夫何
文日勝而質滅名競起而實亡以文為職
===

同而求異以文資講論者不求近而求逺
體雖不同同於厭正大以立門戶心雖不
同同於竊虛名以事捷徑離真失正之害
在今時亦或有之不特如程子所云而已
是何足以鳴

導之神不在文而在心倡率之機不在下

…the dynasty’s government, which examines antiquity and honors learning, surpasses those of former ages. In educating people through the schools and obtaining scholars through the examination system, it esteems only learning in the Classics; all examination categories devoted to lyric poetry and rhapsodies have been abolished. Thus, our predecessors renowned for their writing honored the teaching of the Book of Odes without falling into simple-mindedness; the teaching of the Book of Documents without falling into credulity; the teaching of the Book of Music without falling into extravagance; the teaching of the Book of Changes without falling into perniciousness; the teaching of the Book of Rites without falling into excessive punctiliousness; and the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals without falling into disorder. If we assess these men through their writings, and their age through its prevailing practices, we cannot deny the efficacy of the moral guidance and exemplary leadership exercised at that time.
Why, then, does literary ornament daily prevail while substance disappears, and why do reputations arise in rivalry while genuine worth vanishes? Those whose official duties involve writing seek obscurity rather than clarity; those who use writing to discuss affairs of government seek divergence rather than agreement; those who use writing to support scholarly discussion seek the remote rather than what lies close at hand. Though their styles differ, they share a distaste for uprightness and breadth of vision, setting up separate schools of their own. Though their intentions differ, they share a desire to steal empty reputations and pursue shortcuts to advancement. The harm of departing from truth and losing rectitude may also be found in our own time: it is not confined to the circumstances of which Master Cheng spoke. How could such writing suffice to proclaim the flourishing of our illustrious age and serve as a model for later generations?
I have heard that the transforming power of moral guidance resides in the heart, not in writing, and that the impetus for exemplary leadership lies with those above, not those below. If one could truly unify moral principles so as to bring customs into accord, and teach people the direction [?] …

…the method: give priority to capacity and discernment over literary accomplishment, and show people the proper standards for acceptance and rejection. From the nearby imperial court to distant village communities, from grand imperial edicts to minor correspondence, let everything strive for uprightness and dignity rather than novelty and extravagance. Let those engaged in writing proceed from the breadth of the three masters to seek the concision of the four masters; from the concision of the four masters to seek the teachings of the Six Classics; and from the teachings of the Six Classics to seek further the intention with which the sages of high antiquity wrote only when they could not do otherwise. For those who govern, the difficulty lies less in responding to changes throughout the realm than in deciding how to act at its critical junctures. When the first stirrings of events appear, their possible transformations are endless. If those responding strike precisely at the crucial point, they can turn danger into security and disorder into good government, and extinguish upheaval before it takes shape. Yet if their deliberations are unsound or their actions careless, a discrepancy as slight as a hair’s breadth may produce vastly different outcomes—success or failure, advantage or adversity. You gentlemen have issued a policy question in the autumn Provincial Examination, graciously asking us students about the upheavals caused by the Tang military governorships. Surely your purpose is to take past events as a warning for the future? I am an ignorant student who subsists on bean leaves: what could I know of the court’s deliberations? Yet even the man of Qi knew to worry about Heaven, and the widow did not concern herself with her weaving, so much did she fear for the state. How much more should this be true of one encouraged by the nurturing of talent celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood” and “The Oak and the Bushes”! How could I dare not devote my whole mind to answering?

Upheavals at court were exceedingly numerous, but the repeated disloyalty of the military governorships was especially grave. Were there no men fit to be entrusted with service in Weibo and the other military governorships? 世巨猾逋誅不能取魏豈非遣使之辱命
乎李惟岳世濟其凶兵馬使王武俊誅之
其功大矣雖授之節鉞胡為不可而乃儕
===
之康日知之功賞以恒冀之團練遂使反
間得入三鎮連衡胡氏以為事幾已至應
之失宜朝廷忽事之過也朱泚奉天之圍
李懷光千里赴難其勲盛矣苟召入一見
足慰其心乃謬聽盧杞之諧使之屯長安
之便橋遂使心懷怏怏恃衆為亂後詔許
歸葬宥其一子亦當時處置之失也嗚呼
神堯以一旅取天下而子孫不能以天下
取河北其始也豈遂至於此哉特以變故

punctuated: 黨，互相表裏，治兵完城，不供貢賦。朝廷之上厭苦兵革，遂不能制，豈非姑息之太過乎？承嗣既叛，平盧、成德表以請討矣。當時驅策有方，豈不能成蕩平之功乎？而中使馬承倩責詔往勞，輕其所遺，擲出道中，肆為詬詈，遂使諸鎮解體，按兵不進。終唐之世，巨猾逋誅，不能取魏，豈非遣使之辱命乎？李惟岳世濟其凶，兵馬使王武俊誅之，其功大矣。雖授之節鉞，胡為不可？而乃儕之康日知之功，賞以恒冀之團練，遂使反間得入，三鎮連衡。胡氏以為事幾已至，應之失宜，朝廷忽事之過也。朱泚奉天之圍，李懷光千里赴難，其勲盛矣。苟召入一見，足慰其心，乃謬聽盧杞之諧，使之屯長安之便橋，遂使心懷怏怏，恃衆為亂。後詔許歸葬，宥其一子，亦當時處置之失也。嗚呼！神堯以一旅取天下，而子孫不能以天下取河北，其始也豈遂至於此哉？特以變故
translation_en:
…followers, supporting one another, drilling their troops and strengthening their cities, while withholding tribute and taxes. Those at court, weary of warfare, consequently could not control them. Was this not excessive indulgence? After Chengsi rebelled, Pinglu and Chengde submitted memorials requesting permission to attack him. Had the court directed them properly at that time, could it not have achieved complete pacification? Yet the palace envoy Ma Chengqian, sent with an edict [?] to commend them, disdained their gifts, flung them out onto the road, and freely hurled abuse. This caused the military commands to fall away from one another and hold their troops back without advancing. Throughout the remainder of the Tang dynasty, the great villain escaped execution, and the court could not recover Wei. Was this not a case of an envoy disgracing his commission?

Li Weiyue perpetuated his family's wickedness, and Commander Wang Wujun killed him—a great achievement indeed. Even granting him the insignia of a military commissioner would have been entirely appropriate. Instead, the court ranked his achievement alongside that of Kang Rizhi and rewarded him with the post of Military Training Commissioner of Heng and Ji. This allowed enemy intrigues to take effect, and the three military commands formed an alliance. Master Hu considered this a failure by the court to take affairs seriously: the decisive moment had arrived, but its response was ill judged.

When Zhu Ci besieged Fengtian, Li Huaiguang traveled a thousand li to come to the rescue. His service was outstanding. Simply summoning him for a single audience would have been enough to reassure him. Yet the court mistakenly heeded Lu Qi's words [?] and ordered him to encamp at Bian Bridge near Chang'an. This filled him with resentment, and, relying on his troops, he rebelled. The later edict permitting his remains to be returned for burial and pardoning one of his sons was also a failure in the handling of affairs at the time.

Alas! Shenyao, the founding emperor of Tang, took the empire with a single small force, yet his descendants, with the resources of the entire empire, could not take Hebei. At the outset, how could matters have been destined to reach such a pass? It was simply because unforeseen crises…

title: 嘉靖四年順天府鄉試錄
text:
起於須臾而應接失於倉卒加之以武□
解紐制將非人是以既乏先見之知遂遺
後事之悔耳
國朝法令精明軍政嚴肅各省有都司沿邊
有諸鎮兵皆土著將則
朝除上有易制之權下無世襲之患如唐之
河北諸鎮萬萬無是而近日甘肅大同稍
為不靖賴我
聖天子神謀宸斷旋復克平然無將之戒漸不
===
可長誠有如執事所慮者愚則以為幾者
事之微也古人於事不見是圖况其著乎
故幾之来也迎而治之則易為力盖彼方
翹首俟吾之斷以卜其張弛而吾之應之
賞功罰罪之典適以壓服其心厭足其意
不惟有以止亂而益成吾之治矣矧兩鎮
之變非有河北之桀黠特以廩賜之不繼
勞逸之不均倡狂跳踯遂陷大戮然亦豈
聖世之所宜有哉故為今之計宜明賞罰之法
